title: Given item weights and values and a knapsack capacity, maximize total value where each item may be taken at most once (0 or 1).
shortTitle: 0/1 Knapsack — maximize value under a weight capacity

s1_definition.profdef: Bounded-knapsack DP where dp[c] is the best value achievable with capacity c. We process each item once and sweep capacities DOWNWARD (from capacity to the item weight) so each item is used at most once: dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c−weight]+value). Time O(items · capacity), space O(capacity).
s1_definition.analogy: A treasury officer at National Bank of India must load a secure cash van that holds a limited total weight, choosing among sealed cassettes each with a weight and a value. Each cassette can be loaded at most once. For every capacity she asks whether adding this cassette beats leaving it out.
s1_definition.oneliner: Each item once ⇒ sweep capacity DOWNWARD; dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c−w]+v).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Bounded-knapsack DP where dp[c] is the best value achievable with capacity c. We process each item once and sweep capacities DOWNWARD (from capacity to the item weight) so each item is used at most once: dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c−weight]+value). Time O(items · capacity), space O(capacity).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A treasury officer at National Bank of India must load a secure cash van that holds a limited total weight, choosing among sealed cassettes each with a weight and a value. Each cassette can be loaded at most once. For every capacity she asks whether adding this cassette beats leaving it out.

**One line to remember:** Each item once ⇒ sweep capacity DOWNWARD; dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c−w]+v).

sections.s2_technical:
Create a one-dimensional dp of size capacity+1 initialized to zero. For each item, iterate capacity from the full capacity down to the item's weight, relaxing dp[c] with dp[c−weight]+value. For example: `for (int c = capacity; c >= w[i]; c--) dp[c] = Math.max(dp[c], dp[c - w[i]] + v[i]);`.

The downward sweep is the crucial 0/1 detail. Going downward means dp[c−weight] still refers to a state that has not yet included the current item, so each item is counted at most once. Sweeping upward would let the same item be reused, which is the unbounded knapsack instead.

The time is O(items · capacity) and space is O(capacity) after the one-dimensional reduction from the natural two-dimensional table. A senior nuance is that knapsack capacity is pseudo-polynomial (polynomial in the numeric capacity, not its bit length), which is why huge capacities need different techniques.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a cash van has a strict weight limit, and the treasury must choose which sealed cassettes to load to maximize the transported value. Each cassette is unique and loaded at most once. This is exactly how 0/1 Knapsack works.

Problem 2 — Loading the same cassette twice is physically impossible, so reuse must be forbidden. This is exactly why capacities are swept downward.

The mini-project builds a `VanLoader`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input weights are one, three, four, five with values one, four, five, seven and capacity seven.

Step 1: dp starts all zero, meaning no value loaded at any capacity.

Step 2: Processing the weight-one item downward sets dp of capacities one through seven to one.

Step 3: Processing the weight-three value-four item lifts mid capacities, for example dp of four becomes five by combining weights one and three.

Step 4: Processing the weight-four value-five and weight-five value-seven items relaxes further, and dp of seven reaches nine by combining weights three and four.

Step 5: The final answer at capacity seven is nine.

```text
2026-10-27T02:00:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Treasury Van Loader (0/1 Knapsack)
2026-10-27T02:00:00Z [INFO] Best value for capacity 7 = 9
2026-10-27T02:00:00Z [INFO] capacity 7 → 9
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  dp[0..7] = 0
  item(w=1,v=1): dp[1..7]=1
  item(w=3,v=4): dp[4]=5 ...
  item(w=4,v=5): dp[7]=max(dp[7], dp[3]+5) ...
  item(w=5,v=7): dp[7]=max(dp[7], dp[2]+7) ...
  capacity swept DOWNWARD ⇒ each item used once ; dp[7]=9
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The zero-one knapsack is a bounded dynamic programming problem. I define dp of c as the best total value I can achieve with a remaining capacity of c, starting from all zeros. I process each item once, and for each item I sweep the capacity from the full capacity down to the item's weight, relaxing dp of c with dp of c minus the weight plus the value.

The direction of the sweep is the whole trick. Sweeping downward guarantees that dp of c minus the weight still refers to a state that has not yet included the current item, so every item is used at most once, which is the zero-one rule. If I swept upward instead, the same item could be reused, and that would be the unbounded knapsack.

In my project at National Bank of India, a cash van had a strict weight limit and the treasury had to pick which sealed cassettes to load to maximize the transported value, where each cassette could be loaded only once. I used this one-dimensional knapsack with a downward capacity sweep, and I always mention that the complexity is pseudo-polynomial in the capacity, which matters when the capacity is very large.
